225.title: "Abandon all dharmas, come to me alone" (18.66–18.72)
225.hook: the verse many call the Gita's last word, and the question Krishna asks after it
225.tomorrow: Sanjaya's closing; "wherever Krishna and Arjuna are" (18.73–18.78)
225.howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, Gita 18.66 is honored as the charama shloka, the final verse, and is central to the teaching of surrender (prapatti); teachers in other traditions also give it a central place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yathecchasi, I have told you, now do as you choose. Reflect fully, then decide, and you are deeply loved. Your line was he hands it back. Today, the verse that comes right after. Day two hundred twenty-five.

A child learning to swim. For weeks: kick like this, cup your hands like that, turn your head, breathe. Rules and more rules. Then one day the parent stands in the water, arms open, and says: forget all that. Just come to me. I've got you. The rules weren't wrong. But there's a moment when trust does what technique can't. In one Hindu tradition, the verse right after Krishna hands the choice back is that moment. They call it the charama shloka, the final verse.
screen: `KICK, CUP, TURN, BREATHE.` → `THEN: FORGET ALL THAT.` → `COME TO ME. I'VE GOT YOU.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-six. Abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge. I will free you from all wrongs. Do not grieve. Sarva-dharman parityajya, mam ekam sharanam vraja. Commentators have argued over every word. What does abandon all dharmas mean, after a whole book about doing your dharma? Here's who says what. The Sri Vaishnava tradition, which follows Ramanuja, calls this the charama shloka and reads it as surrender, prapatti: stop relying on your own efforts to save yourself, and rely on God's grace alone. Shankara reads it as renouncing all actions and taking refuge in the one self. Other teachers read dharmas here as your anxieties about merit and demerit, not your duties: keep acting, but let go of the scorekeeping. However the first line is read, the verse ends with two words: ma shuchah. Do not grieve. The Gita began with Arjuna grieving, and it ends with Krishna telling him not to. Then verses sixty-seven to seventy-one are about passing the teaching on. Don't tell it to someone who doesn't want to hear it. Whoever shares it with those who love it is most dear. Even someone who only listens to it with faith, without scoffing, finds freedom. And then verse seventy-two. After all that, Krishna asks: Have you heard this with a focused mind, Arjuna? Is your confusion gone? The teacher checks in. That's the last instruction: come for refuge, don't grieve, and did you hear me? That's the word today: abandon all dharmas.
screen: `ABANDON ALL DHARMAS, COME TO ME.` · `THREE READINGS, ONE VERSE.` · `DO NOT GRIEVE.` · `HAVE YOU HEARD THIS, ARJUNA?` · then, large: `ABANDON ALL DHARMAS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice what you're carrying today. The rules you're keeping, the scores you're tracking, the ways you're trying to get it all right. Let yourself feel the weight of it. Then, just for these two minutes, set it down. Remember the swimming child, and the open arms in the water. You don't have to believe anything to try this. Just let the weight rest for a moment, and hear the verse's last two words: do not grieve. The bell holds the time.
Sharanam, refuge, shelter. Gita eighteen, sixty-six: abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge; I will free you from all wrongs; do not grieve.
Your line: the last instruction. Today, when you catch yourself keeping score, set it down for one breath, and hear the last two words: do not grieve. Day two hundred twenty-five.

226.title: Sanjaya's closing; "wherever Krishna and Arjuna are" (18.73–18.78)
226.hook: the Gita ends not with Krishna, but with the narrator who's been watching all along
226.tomorrow: The whole Gita in one session
226.howItsDone: When Hindus recite the whole Gita, the reading closes with Sanjaya's words in 18.74–18.78; the last verse, on fortune and victory wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, is sometimes recited on its own as a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sharanam, abandon all dharmas, come to me alone, do not grieve. Your line was the last instruction. And Krishna asked: is your confusion gone? Today, Arjuna answers, and the book ends. Day two hundred twenty-six.

Go back to the very first verse. An old blind king, Dhritarashtra, sits in his palace far from the battlefield. His sons lead one army. His nephews, Arjuna and his brothers, lead the other. He can't see, so he asks his charioteer Sanjaya, who has been given the gift of seeing far off: what are they doing? The entire Gita, every word, has been Sanjaya's answer. The king was hoping for news of his sons. What he got was this. Today, Sanjaya speaks for the last time.
screen: `A BLIND KING IN HIS PALACE.` → `WHAT ARE THEY DOING?` → `THE WHOLE GITA IS THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, Arjuna. Verse seventy-three: my confusion is gone. I've found my memory again, through your grace. I stand firm, my doubts are gone. I will do what you say. Karishye vachanam tava. It's his whole journey in one breath. In chapter one he was shaking, his bow slipping from his hand. Now he stands. Notice he says memory. Some readers hear in that word a hint that wisdom is less something learned than something remembered. Then Sanjaya. Verse seventy-four: I have heard this wondrous conversation between Krishna and the great-souled Arjuna, and my hair stands on end. Verse seventy-five: by the grace of Vyasa I heard this highest secret, this yoga, from Krishna, the lord of yoga himself, speaking it directly. Vyasa is the sage the Mahabharata names as its author. Verse seventy-six: remembering again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue, I rejoice, again and again. Verse seventy-seven: and remembering that astonishing form of Hari, great is my wonder, and I rejoice again and again. The narrator can't stop remembering. And verse seventy-eight, the last verse of the Gita. Wherever there is Krishna, the lord of yoga, wherever there is Arjuna, the archer, there is fortune, victory, well-being and sound judgment. That is my conviction. It's quietly pointed. Sanjaya is telling a king who wanted his own sons to win exactly where victory lies. The war still has to be fought; the Mahabharata goes on. But the Gita ends by saying where to look: where the divine and the human act together. That's the word today: Sanjaya's closing.

segments.voice: Sit, and do what Sanjaya does: remember. Let one moment from these seventy days of the Gita come back to you. A picture, a verse, a line you carried. The lamp in a windless place. The upside-down tree. Your own dharma. Let it come fully. Notice if anything in you rejoices. Then let another come. Again and again. The bell holds the time.
Sanjaya's closing. Gita eighteen, seventy-eight: wherever Krishna, lord of yoga, and Arjuna, the archer, are, there is fortune, victory, well-being and sound judgment.
Your line: victory is there. Today, before one task, picture the two in the chariot: the divine and the human, acting together. Day two hundred twenty-six.

227.title: The whole Gita in one session
227.hook: eighteen chapters, seven hundred verses, one man in a chariot, in five minutes
227.tomorrow: Your twelve verses · pick the ones that stayed
227.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the whole Bhagavad Gita on special days such as Gita Jayanti, sometimes in a single sitting and sometimes over eighteen days, a chapter a day; teachers sometimes divide it into three sets of six chapters.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sanjaya's closing. Wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is fortune and victory. Your line was victory is there. That was the last verse. This is graduation week. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

Eighteen chapters. About seven hundred verses, as tradition counts them. One conversation in a chariot, parked between two armies. For about seventy days this path has walked through it a few verses at a time, the way a long road trip goes one town at a time: this river, that bridge, the night the car broke down. At the end of a trip like that, it helps to pull over, open the map, and trace the whole route with a finger. That's today. No new verse. The whole route, at once.

One traditional teaching aid divides the Gita into three sets of six chapters. The first six are mostly about action. Chapter one: two armies, and Arjuna sinks down in the chariot. Chapter two: Krishna answers. The self is never born and never dies. You have a right to your action, not to its fruit. Chapters three to five: act, but offer the action. Whenever dharma declines, Krishna says, I come. Chapter six: sit, steady the mind, like a lamp in a windless place. The middle six are mostly about devotion. Chapters seven to nine: Krishna says all this is strung on me like pearls on a thread, and whoever offers a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, I accept it. Chapter ten: wherever you see glory, it's a spark of mine. Chapter eleven: Arjuna asks to see, and sees the cosmic form, and is terrified, and asks for the familiar face back. Chapter twelve: devotion, the ladder, and priya, the one dear to me. The last six are mostly about knowledge. Chapter thirteen: kshetra, the body is the field, and the one light shines in every field. Fourteen: the three threads. Fifteen: the upside-down tree and the highest person. Sixteen: the divine and the demonic, and the three gates. Seventeen: shraddha, faith follows nature, and sat. And eighteen, the graduation chapter: let go of the fruit, not the act. Reflect fully, then do as you choose. Abandon all dharmas, come to me, do not grieve. And Arjuna stands up. Action, devotion, knowledge. The book weaves them together. That's the word today: the whole Gita in one session.

Now let the whole conversation pass through you, without words, just the shape of it. Collapse. Questions. A vision. Love. Understanding. Standing up. Let yourself sit in the chariot for a moment, in the space between the question and the answer. The bell holds the time.
Gita, song. Eighteen chapters, about seven hundred verses, the song of the Blessed One, often read as three sixes: action, devotion and knowledge.
Your line: you read it. Today, tell one person, in one sentence, what the Gita is about. See what you say. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

228.title: Your twelve verses · pick the ones that stayed
228.hook: out of seven hundred verses, a dozen have probably already moved in
228.tomorrow: The Gita in your week · one verse per day going forward
228.howItsDone: Many Hindus learn a few Gita verses by heart, often from parents or grandparents, and recite them in hard moments; some children learn whole chapters, and Gita recitation contests are held in parts of India.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gita, the whole Gita in one session. Action, devotion, knowledge, and Arjuna standing up. Your line was you read it. What did you say when you told someone? Today, you make it yours. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

A song comes on in a grocery store, one nobody ever sat down to memorize, and a shopper in the cereal aisle is mouthing every word, fifteen years later. Some lines just stay. Books can work the same way: read a whole one, and a few lines refuse to leave. Some Hindu families carry the Gita like that: not the whole book, but a handful of verses learned by heart, often from a parent or grandparent, and said when they're needed. Today, you pick yours.
screen: `THE SONGS THAT STAYED.` → `A FEW LINES THAT WON'T LEAVE.` → `TODAY, PICK YOURS.`

segments.voice: A Gita verse is called a shloka. Much of the Gita is written in a meter of four short lines, eight syllables each, made to be chanted and remembered. The Ramayana tells a story about how the shloka was born: the poet Valmiki saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of birds, and his grief, shoka, came out of him as the first shloka. Grief turned into verse. In Hindi, a verse learned by heart can be called kanthastha: held in the throat. Here are twelve verses from our path, as candidates. Two, twenty: the self is never born and never dies. Two, forty-seven: your right is to the action, not to its fruit. Two, forty-eight: yoga is evenness of mind. Three, thirty-five: your own dharma, even imperfect. Four, seven: whenever dharma declines, I come. Six, five: lift yourself by yourself; you're your own friend and your own enemy. Six, nineteen: a lamp in a windless place. Nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, some water, offered with love. Twelve, thirteen: free from hate, friendly to all. Thirteen, thirty-three: one sun lights the whole world. Eighteen, sixty-three: reflect fully, then do as you choose. Eighteen, sixty-six: come to me for refuge; do not grieve. Keep the ones that stayed. Drop the ones that didn't. Swap in any others that caught you. There's no correct twelve. The Gita's own teaching fits here: your own, even imperfect, is better than someone else's list, perfectly chosen. That's the word today: your twelve verses.

segments.voice: Sit, and let the twelve drift past you once more, without trying. The self that never dies. The right to act. The lamp. The leaf and the flower. The one sun. Do not grieve. Notice which one your mind keeps returning to. Don't argue with it. That's your first verse. Say it silently a few times, in your own words, and let it settle in your throat. The bell holds the time.
Shloka, a verse. A shloka, made to be held in the throat; out of about seven hundred, the dozen that stayed with you.
Your line: yours. Today, write down the one verse that came back first, in your own words, and put it where you'll see it tomorrow morning. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

229.title: The Gita in your week · one verse per day going forward
229.hook: the reading is done; the carrying starts
229.tomorrow: Gita path in the world: Gandhi, Thoreau, Tilak, Vivekananda
229.howItsDone: Many Hindus read or recite the Gita regularly: a few verses each morning, a chapter a day across eighteen days, or a full recitation on Gita Jayanti in the month of Margashirsha; svadhyaya, one's own study of sacred texts, is counted as a spiritual discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shloka, your twelve verses, the ones that stayed. Your line was yours. Did you write one down where you'd see it this morning? Today, what to do with them next. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

People who finish a marathon often say the strangest part is the Monday after. For months, every morning had a shape: the run, the plan, the number. Then it's done, and the morning is suddenly empty. Some people never run again. Others find a small, steady habit that keeps the thing alive. Tomorrow and the next day finish this camp. But the Gita wasn't written to be finished. In Hindu tradition it's read again, and again, for a lifetime. So today is about the Monday after.
screen: `THE MONDAY AFTER THE MARATHON.` → `THE MORNING SUDDENLY EMPTY.` → `A SMALL, STEADY HABIT.`

segments.voice: Hindu tradition has a word for this: svadhyaya. Sva, your own; adhyaya, study, reading, recitation. Self-study. It's older than the Gita, and the Gita names it twice. In chapter sixteen it's one of the divine qualities. In chapter seventeen, the discipline of speech includes the regular recitation of sacred texts. The yoga tradition later lists svadhyaya among its daily observances too. So reading isn't something you do once. It's a practice, like the sit. Here's a simple shape for the week. Take your twelve verses and give each day one. Monday, the self that never dies. Tuesday, your right is to the action. Wednesday, the lamp. Whatever your twelve are. Read the verse in the morning. Carry it through the day. At night, ask: where did it show up? After twelve days, start again. The same verses will say different things in a different month. That's normal. The Gita itself circles back: letting go of the fruit comes up in chapter two, again in three, again in five, and once more in eighteen. There are older rhythms too. Some families read one chapter a day, finishing the Gita in eighteen days. Some recite a chapter on a set day each week. Many temples and homes celebrate Gita Jayanti, the Gita's birthday, each winter in the month of Margashirsha, often with a full recitation. You can join any of these, or just keep one verse a day. The point is the carrying. The Gita becomes yours not when you finish it, but when a line of it turns up uninvited, halfway through a hard phone call. That's the word today: the Gita in your week.
screen: `SVADHYAYA: YOUR OWN STUDY.` · `ONE VERSE A DAY.` · `A CHAPTER A DAY, OR GITA JAYANTI.` · `IT SHOWS UP UNINVITED.` · then, large: `THE GITA IN YOUR WEEK.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose tomorrow's verse. Just one, from your twelve. Let it come to mind in your own words. Then picture tomorrow: waking, the first hour, the hardest meeting, dinner, the drive home. Place the verse somewhere in that day, like leaving a note in a coat pocket for yourself to find. Then rest, and let it wait there. The bell holds the time.
Svadhyaya, one's own study. One verse a day, read in the morning, carried all day, and started again when the twelve are done.
Your line: carry. Tonight, before sleep, say tomorrow's verse once. In the morning, say it again. Then carry it. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

230.title: Gita path in the world: Gandhi, Thoreau, Tilak, Vivekananda
230.hook: a book spoken in a chariot ended up in a jail cell in Mandalay and a cabin by Walden Pond
230.howItsDone: Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga, Tilak's Gita Rahasya and Vivekananda's talks are still widely read in India, and many Hindus know the Gita partly through these modern readings as well as the classical commentaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: svadhyaya, the Gita in your week. One verse a day, read in the morning, carried all day. Your line was carry. Did today's verse show up? Today, some people who carried it very far. Day two hundred thirty.

A young law student from Gujarat is studying in London in the late eighteen-eighties. Two brothers he has met there ask him to read the Gita with them. Embarrassed, he admits he's never read it, not even in Sanskrit or Gujarati. So he first meets it in an English poem, Edwin Arnold's The Song Celestial. His name is Mohandas Gandhi. Back in India, in Pune, a newspaper editor will one day make the Gita his life's argument. And some forty years before that, in a cabin by a pond in Massachusetts, an American was reading it in the mornings.
screen: `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `AN ENGLISH POEM.` → `A CABIN BY A POND.`

segments.voice: Start at the pond. The first English translation of the Gita, by Charles Wilkins, appeared in 1785, and it reached New England. Henry David Thoreau took it to Walden. In Walden he wrote: "In the morning I bathe my intellect in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta." His friend Emerson loved it too. Then Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a leader of India's independence movement. Jailed by the British in Mandalay, in Burma, he wrote a long Marathi commentary, the Gita Rahasya, the secret of the Gita, published in 1915. His argument: the Gita's heart is karma yoga, energetic action in the world, not withdrawal from it. Swami Vivekananda, who spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, read the Gita as a call to strength. He loved Krishna's first sharp words to Arjuna in chapter two: don't give in to weakness; stand up. And Gandhi. He came to call the Gita his mother. In 1929 he finished a Gujarati translation he titled Anasakti Yoga, the yoga of non-attachment. He read the battle as the war inside every person, and drew from it selfless action and nonviolence. Tilak and Gandhi read the same book and disagreed, sharply, about whether it could justify force. That argument is still alive. Others read the Gita critically, like B. R. Ambedkar, whom we met a few days ago. All of them took it seriously enough to wrestle with it. The Gita left the chariot a long time ago. It's been in jail cells, cabins, ashrams and lecture halls. That's the word today: Gita path in the world.

231.howItsDone: In traditional Hindu education, the end of study was marked by samavartana, the student's ceremonial return home, and the teacher's final advice in Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 is still recited at some convocations in India; many Hindus mark finishing the Gita with a full recitation or a small puja.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anasakti, the Gita in the world. Thoreau at the pond, Tilak in a cell, Vivekananda, Gandhi. Your line was who else carried it. Did someone tell you what carried them? Today, the last day of the camp. Day two hundred thirty-one.

In ancient India, a student lived for years in the teacher's house, learning the Vedas by heart. When the studies were done, there was a ceremony called samavartana: the return home. The student bathed, put on new clothes, and the teacher gave a last talk. One version of that talk survives in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Speak the truth. Practice dharma. Don't neglect your study. Treat your mother, your father, your teacher and your guest as the divine. Then the student walked home, carrying it all. Today is your samavartana.

segments.voice: Look at what you're carrying. It started with twenty-one words, back in camp one. Namaste. Om. Dharma. Shanti. Pranam. Ganesha. Mantra. Puja. Karma. Atman. Brahman. Guru. Japa. Arti. Seva. Bhakti. Ahimsa. Maya. Moksha. Satsang. And the twenty-first, the Gita itself, the mountain ahead, with its line: you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Then the stories, then the practices. And then, for seventy-five days, the text itself, a few verses at a time. Chapter one, a man collapsing in a chariot. Chapter eighteen, the same man standing up and saying, my confusion is gone. This last week drew it together. The last instruction: do not grieve. Sanjaya's closing: wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is victory. The whole book in one session. Shloka: your twelve verses, chosen by you. One verse a day, going forward. And the people who carried it before you. Here's what's worth saying plainly. Plenty of people keep a Gita on the shelf and never read it through. You have. Not in a weekend, not by skimming, but slowly, one piece of the conversation at a time. That counts. Tomorrow the path goes deeper. Camp five is the depths: the Upanishads, the texts the Gita itself draws on. We start with the Isha Upanishad, eighteen verses in a week, and its first line: all this is pervaded by the Lord. But today, just take the bath, put on the new clothes, and walk home carrying it. That's the word today: graduation.

Then let the Gita come as a single picture: the chariot, the two, the dawn over the field. Then bring to mind your one verse for today. Hold it. You don't have to do anything with it. Just notice that it's yours now. The bell holds the time.
Graduation. In the old tradition, samavartana, the student's return home, with a last teaching: speak the truth, practice dharma, don't neglect your study.
Your line: you actually read it. Today, let yourself feel that, just once, without rushing past it. Tomorrow, the depths. Day two hundred thirty-one.
